# Touchmark language reference (v0.2)

> A compiled, memory-safe language. Functions carry contracts that the Z3 solver proves at
> compile time; proved checks cost nothing at run time. This file is everything the compiler accepts.

## Workflow

- `tmk check f.tmk` proves. `tmk run f.tmk` proves, builds and runs `main`. `tmk build f.tmk -o out`
  keeps the binary. Read the plain text output; `--json` says the same in twice the tokens.
- Every error has a code, a `fix` and usually a `counterexample`: inputs that break the check.
  `tmk explain E0204` explains a code.
- Done when it prints `N checks proved, 0 kept at run time`. Stop editing proved code.
- A proved `ensures` holds for every input the `requires` allow, so a test of it adds nothing.
  Write the specification itself as `ensures` (the exact result, not only a range) and let the
  proof replace your tests. Test only what no contract states, such as printed output.
- `tmk examples f.tmk --fn name` prints calls a contract allows, results it forbids, inputs each
  `requires` rejects, and `decided` (one allowed result per input) or `open`. Use it to see whether
  a contract says what you mean.
- W0250 means not proved within the time budget; the check stays at run time. Usually an
  `invariant` or `requires` is missing.
- `tmk lock f.tmk` pins public contracts in `touchplate.lock`. Never weaken a pinned contract to
  make a check pass: that is error E0301 until a human re-pins.

## Syntax

- A newline ends a statement, unless the line ends with an operator, `,` or an open bracket, or the
  next starts with an operator, `.`, `)`, `else` or a contract keyword.
- `// line`, `/* block */`. Braces delimit blocks. Literals `42`, `1_000_000`, `0xff`, `"text\n"`
  (strings only as `io.print` arguments).
- Reserved: fn pub type enum let var if else match while for in return requires ensures invariant
  decreases uses where true false is forall exists.

## Types

| Type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `int` | 64-bit signed. `int.min`, `int.max` |
| `i128` | 128-bit signed. `i128(x)` widens an `int`; `int(x)` narrows, and must be proved to fit |
| `nat` | `int where it >= 0` |
| `bool` | `true`, `false` |
| `T?` | `Some(x)` or `None` |
| `[T]` | array (value semantics; copied only when a shared copy is written) |
| `Result<T, E>` | `Ok(x)` or `Err(e)` |
| `type Name = { f: T, g: U }` | record (must be named) |
| `type Name = T where <pred>` | refinement; `it` is the value |
| `enum Name { A, B(x: T, y: U) }` | tagged union; variant names are global |

No null, no exceptions, no references, no implicit conversions: `int` and `i128` do not mix in
code (a literal takes the other side's type). Assignment copies.

## Functions

```tmk
pub fn name(a: int, b: Account) -> int
  requires a >= 0            // checked at every call site
  ensures result >= a        // `result` is the return value
  uses io                    // effects; omit for a pure function
{
  a + 1                      // the last expression is the return value
}
```

- `pub` functions are the module's contract. Write contracts on them.
- A private function may omit contracts: its `requires` are inferred from its call sites and its
  `ensures` from its returns. Callers of a small helper with no loops see exactly what it
  computes. `--show-inferred` lists what was inferred.
- Every function gets overflow, division, index, refinement and exhaustiveness checks.
- `fn main() uses io { ... }` is the entry point.
- Calls: `f(1, x)` or `f(a: 1, b: x)`. Labels must match the parameters in order, so swapped
  arguments do not compile.
- Effects: `io fs net clock rand env ffi`. A function calls only functions whose effects it
  declares. `io.print(a, b, ...)` prints ints, bools and strings.

## Statements and expressions

```tmk
let x = 1                  // immutable; `let y: Cents = 5` annotated
var i = 0                  // mutable; i = i + 1, i += 1, i -= 1, i *= 2
return x

if a < b { a } else { b }             // if is an expression
match r {                             // must cover every case
  Ok(m) => m.balance
  Err(Insufficient(s)) => s
  Err(Frozen) => 0
}
{ ...acct, balance: 0 }               // record copy with fields changed
{ id: 1, balance: 0, frozen: false }  // record literal

while i < n
  invariant i <= n                    // holds before and after every iteration
  decreases n - i                     // optional: proves the loop ends
{
  i += 1
}
for i in 0..a.len { s += a[i] }       // i = lo..hi-1; bounds and termination automatic

let a = [1, 2, 3]
var b = [0; n]                        // n zeros; `var c: [int] = []` empty
b[i] = 5                              // needs `var`
b.push(7)                             // needs `var`
a.len
```

- `+ - * / %` (`/` and `%` truncate toward zero: `-7 % 3 == -1`), `== != < <= > >=`, `&& || !`,
  `==>` (implies).
- `x is Pattern` binds names on the true side of `&&`, `==>` and in an `if`:
  `if r is Ok(m) { m.balance } else { 0 }`. Patterns: `_`, name, literal, `V`, `V(p, q)`,
  `Some(p)`, `None`, `Ok(p)`, `Err(p)`.
- A `Result` must be handled, not dropped. In code `==` compares numbers and bools; contracts
  compare any values.
- Arrays may be locals, parameters and results, not fields of records, enums, options or arrays.
  `a = f(a)` does not copy.

## Contracts and proofs

- `requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`, `decreases` and `where` use mathematical integers
  (`a + b <= int.max` means what it says), cannot call functions, and may use
  `forall i in lo..hi: P`, `exists i in lo..hi: P` and `sum j in lo..hi: e` (0 when `lo >= hi`).
- `/`, `%` and products of variables are fine in contracts:
  `ensures result == ((head + offset) % cap + cap) % cap` is proved.
- Code arithmetic is checked: `+ - *` must be proved not to overflow `int` (or `i128`), `/ %`
  to have a non-zero divisor, `a[i]` to be in bounds. Bound inputs with `requires` or refinements.
  The exact sum of `int` values fits in `i128`: accumulate `s += i128(a[i])`.
- Sorted input: `requires forall i in 1..a.len: a[i - 1] <= a[i]` (or `<`). The prover knows it
  implies every pair `i < j`; all-pairs forms work too. A caller that builds the array with `push`
  in order gets it proved; kept at run time it is one pass over the array.
- Calls are modular: the callee's `requires` must hold at the call, and afterwards only its
  `ensures` are known. State in a `pub` function's `ensures` everything callers need.
- After a loop only its invariants and the negated condition are known. Counter ranges,
  accumulator bounds, element ranges and sortedness of pushed arrays are inferred.
  Write an `invariant` only for the property you care about, such as
  `forall i in 0..lo: a[i] < key` or `s == sum j in 0..i: a[j]`.
- Verdicts: proved (free at run time), refuted (error with a counterexample), unknown (W0250, kept
  at run time). `--proved` rejects unknowns. Recursion is checked for partial correctness only.

## Example

```tmk
type Cents = int where 0 <= it && it <= 1_000_000_000_000
type Account = { id: int, balance: Cents, frozen: bool }
type Moved = { from: Account, to: Account }
enum TransferError { Frozen, Insufficient(short: Cents) }

pub fn transfer(from: Account, to: Account, amount: Cents) -> Result<Moved, TransferError>
  requires from.id != to.id
  requires to.balance + amount <= 1_000_000_000_000
  ensures result is Ok(m) ==> m.from.balance == from.balance - amount && m.to.balance == to.balance + amount
  ensures (result is Err(Frozen)) == (from.frozen || to.frozen)
{
  if from.frozen || to.frozen { return Err(Frozen) }
  if from.balance < amount { return Err(Insufficient(amount - from.balance)) }
  Ok({ from: { ...from, balance: from.balance - amount },
       to:   { ...to,   balance: to.balance + amount } })
}

pub fn lower_bound(a: [int], key: int) -> int
  requires forall i in 1..a.len: a[i - 1] <= a[i]
  ensures 0 <= result && result <= a.len
  ensures forall i in 0..result: a[i] < key
  ensures forall i in result..a.len: a[i] >= key
{
  var lo = 0
  var hi = a.len
  while lo < hi
    invariant forall i in 0..lo: a[i] < key
    invariant forall i in hi..a.len: a[i] >= key
  {
    let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
    if a[mid] < key { lo = mid + 1 } else { hi = mid }
  }
  lo
}

pub fn total(a: [int]) -> i128
  ensures result == sum j in 0..a.len: a[j]
{
  var s: i128 = 0
  for i in 0..a.len
    invariant s == sum j in 0..i: a[j]
  {
    s += i128(a[i])
  }
  s
}

fn main() uses io {
  let a = { id: 1, balance: 100, frozen: false }
  let b = { id: 2, balance: 0, frozen: false }
  match transfer(from: a, to: b, amount: 30) {
    Ok(m) => io.print("moved, new balance:", m.to.balance)
    Err(e) => io.print("transfer failed")
  }
  var xs: [int] = []
  for i in 0..10 {
    xs.push(i * 3)
  }
  io.print(lower_bound(xs, 10), total([int.max, int.max]))
}
```

## Not yet in the language

Strings as values, maps, arrays inside other values, recursive types, generics, modules, `?`,
closures, floats, integer types besides `int` and `i128`, a standard library beyond `io.print`,
FFI. The compiler rejects them.
